title: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
summary: How exact, tiled attention was redesigned for Hopper (warp specialization, ping-pong, GEMM-softmax overlap, accurate FP8) and Blackwell (software exp, conditional rescaling, TMEM, 2-CTA MMA).
outcomes: Compute online softmax block by block, including the rescaling step, and explain why the result is exact
Compute attention FLOPs, HBM bytes and exp-to-matmul time ratios, and utilization from reported TFLOPs/s
Explain FlashAttention-3's producer/consumer warp specialization, ping-pong and intra-warpgroup pipelining
Explain how block quantization and incoherent processing make FP8 attention more accurate
Explain FlashAttention-4's response to Blackwell: software exp2, conditional rescaling, TMEM and 2-CTA MMA

lessons.title: Online softmax: exact attention one block at a time

blocks.md:
Attention for one head computes $S = QK^\top/\sqrt{d}$, takes a row-wise softmax to get $P$, then $O = PV$. With sequence length $N$, $S$ and $P$ are $N \times N$. The naive kernel writes them to HBM (the GPU's off-chip DRAM) and reads them back, and at $N = 8192$ that is 128 MiB per head per matrix in FP16.

The obstacle to keeping everything on chip is the softmax: each output needs the max and the sum over **all** $N$ scores in its row, but the chip's fast memory only holds a few blocks of keys at a time.

**Online softmax** removes that obstacle. FlashAttention (Dao et al., 2022) processes the keys and values in blocks and keeps three running quantities per query row: the max seen so far $m$, the sum of exponentials $l$ (relative to $m$), and an unnormalized output $O$. When a new block raises the max, the old $l$ and $O$ are multiplied by a **correction factor** $e^{m_{old} - m_{new}}$ so everything stays relative to the same max.

blocks.tex: m_j = \max(m_{j-1}, \mathrm{rowmax}(S_j)),\quad l_j = e^{m_{j-1}-m_j}\, l_{j-1} + \mathrm{rowsum}(e^{S_j - m_j}),\quad O_j = e^{m_{j-1}-m_j}\, O_{j-1} + e^{S_j - m_j} V_j
blocks.caption: Block $j$ update, as written in the FlashAttention-2 and FlashAttention-4 papers. After the last block, output $= O / l$.

blocks.md: Here is a tiny example you can check by hand: one query, 6 keys with scores already scaled by $1/\sqrt{d}$, a scalar value per key, and blocks of 2 keys. All numbers below were computed with a script.

blocks.title: One query row, 6 keys, processed in 3 blocks of 2

scenes.caption: Start: the running max $m$ is $-\infty$, the running sum $l$ is 0 and the unnormalized output $O$ is 0. Only the 6 scores and 6 values exist; the kernel will see them 2 at a time.

Block 2 brings a 5, so $m$ jumps from 3 to 5. Old weights shrink by $e^{3-5} = 0.1353$ (0.1353 becomes 0.0183, 1 becomes 0.1353), and $l$ and $O$ shrink by the same factor before the new terms are added.
Block 3 has max 4, below 5, so the correction factor is $e^{0} = 1$ and nothing old changes. New weights 0.0111 and 0.3679 give $l = 1.5824$ and $O = 67.012$.
Final step: divide once, $O/l = 67.012 / 1.5824 = 42.347$. A full softmax over all 6 scores gives exactly the same 42.347: online softmax is exact, not an approximation.

blocks.prompt: Before block 3 the running max is 5. Block 3's scores are 0.5 and 4. What correction factor is applied to the old $l$ and $O$?
blocks.reveal: **1.** The new max is $\max(5, 4) = 5$, unchanged, so the factor is $e^{5-5} = 1$ and the old state is untouched. Rescaling only matters when the max actually grows. Keep this in mind: FlashAttention-4 turns it into an optimization that skips most rescales.

blocks.title: The same loop as code (one query row, scalar values)
blocks.code:
m, l, O = -inf, 0.0, 0.0
for S_blk, V_blk in blocks:
    m_new = max(m, max(S_blk))
    c = exp(m - m_new)          # correction factor
    p = [exp(s - m_new) for s in S_blk]
    l = c * l + sum(p)
    O = c * O + dot(p, V_blk)
    m = m_new
out = O / l                     # one division at the end
lse = m + log(l)                # saved for the backward pass

scenes.caption: Three numbers per query row are all the state the kernel keeps. In the real kernel each is a vector over the $B_r$ rows of a query tile.
Second block: the max rises from 3 to 5, so the correction factor is $e^{3-5} = 0.1353$.
Old $l$ and $O$ are rescaled, then the block's own contribution (computed against the new max) is added.
After the last block: one division gives the output, and the log-sum-exp $L = m + \log l$ is written to memory so the backward pass can rebuild $P$ without storing it.

blocks.md: Online softmax is exact. The running max is only for numerical safety (keeping $e^x$ from overflowing); any consistent reference point gives the same $O/l$. Every FlashAttention version computes the same math; they differ only in how the work is mapped onto the hardware.

FlashAttention-2 (Dao, 2023) kept this math and changed the bookkeeping: it keeps $O$ unnormalized and divides by $l$ once at the end (fewer non-matmul operations), makes the outer loop run over query blocks so different thread blocks can work on different query blocks of the same head, and splits each query block across warps instead of splitting the keys (the "split-K" scheme) so warps no longer exchange partial results through shared memory.

blocks.question: A kernel rescales $O$ by $e^{m_{old}-m_{new}}$ when the max grows but forgets to rescale $l$. What happens to the output in the example above?
options: Nothing, because $l$ only matters for the first block
The output becomes too large, because $l$ is too small
The output becomes too small, because $l$ keeps old terms at their larger, unscaled size
The kernel overflows, because $l$ grows without bound
blocks.explain: Without the factor, block 1's contribution stays at 1.1353 instead of 0.1536 in $l$, so the denominator is too big while $O$ is correct. Dividing gives a value biased toward zero. The bug only shows up when a later block raises the max, which is why it can survive simple tests.

blocks.question: Besides the output tile $O_i$, what does the FlashAttention forward kernel write to HBM for each query row, and why?
options: The full row of $P$, so the backward pass can reuse it
The log-sum-exp $L = m + \log l$, so the backward pass can recompute $P$ from $Q$ and $K$ without storing it
Nothing else; the backward pass recomputes $m$ and $l$ from scratch with a separate reduction
The running max $m$ only, since $l$ can be derived from $O$
blocks.explain: Algorithm 1 in the FlashAttention-3 paper ends by writing $O_i$ and $L_i = m_i + \log(\ell_i)$. One number per row is enough to recompute $P = \exp(S - L)$ block by block in the backward pass, which is how FlashAttention avoids storing the $N \times N$ matrix.

lessons.title: Counting the work: FLOPs, bytes, and the exponential unit

blocks.md: The forward pass of one head does two matrix multiplies, $QK^\top$ and $PV$, each costing $2N^2d$ floating point operations. The papers' benchmark formula is therefore $4 \cdot N^2 \cdot d \cdot \text{heads}$ FLOPs, halved for causal masking (only about half the scores are computed) and multiplied by 2.5 for the backward pass (5 matmuls instead of 2, because $S$ and $P$ are recomputed).

Now the bytes for that same head in FP16 (2 bytes per element). Reading $Q, K, V$ and writing $O$ is $4 \cdot N \cdot d \cdot 2 = 8$ MiB. A naive kernel also writes $S$, reads it back for the softmax, writes $P$ and reads it for $PV$: four passes over 128 MiB each.

blocks.title: HBM traffic for one head, N = 8192, d = 128 (MiB)
labels: Q, K, V in + O out

scenes.caption: Naive attention: 8 MiB of real inputs and outputs, plus 512 MiB of intermediate traffic. The intermediates are 98% of the bytes.

Fused, tiled attention (every FlashAttention version): $S$ and $P$ live only on chip. The ideal traffic is the 8 MiB of unique inputs and outputs. Simplified: real kernels re-read K and V tiles for each query block.

blocks.md: Divide FLOPs by bytes to get **arithmetic intensity**. The naive kernel does $34.4 \times 10^9 / 545 \times 10^6 \approx 63$ FLOPs per byte; the fused kernel's ideal is $4N^2d / 8Nd = N/2 = 4096$. The H100's ridge point is $989 \text{ TFLOPS} / 3.35 \text{ TB/s} \approx 295$ FLOPs per byte, so the naive kernel is memory bound and the fused kernel is, on paper, compute bound. (FlashAttention's IO analysis counts the K and V re-reads as $\Theta(N^2 d^2 / M)$ HBM accesses for on-chip memory size $M$, still far below $\Theta(N^2)$.)

blocks.prompt: FlashAttention-2 already removes the $N^2$ HBM traffic, so attention should run near the tensor-core peak. On an H100, what fraction of the 989 TFLOPS FP16 peak did the FlashAttention-3 authors measure for FlashAttention-2?
blocks.reveal: **About 35%**, versus 80 to 90% for well-tuned matrix multiplies on the same GPU. Being compute bound in the roofline sense is not enough: the kernel also has to keep the tensor cores fed every cycle. FlashAttention-2 uses a synchronous design and Ampere-era instructions, and it pays for the softmax's slow operations in series with the matmuls.

blocks.md: The slow operations are the non-matmul ones, above all the exponential. On the H100, exponentials run on the **multi-function unit (MUFU)** at 16 operations per clock per streaming multiprocessor (SM). Times 132 SMs and 1.83 GHz that is 3.9 TFLOPS, against 989 TFLOPS of FP16 matmul: a 256x gap. Each score costs one exponential but $4d = 512$ matmul FLOPs at $d = 128$, so the exponentials need $256/512 = 0.5$ of the matmul time.

blocks.caption: Per SM per clock: H100 $r_{MMA} = 4096$, $r_{exp} = 16$, so at $d = 128$ the ratio is $4096/8192 = 0.5$. B200 doubles $r_{MMA}$ to 8192 and keeps $r_{exp} = 16$: ratio 1.0.

blocks.title: Exponential time as a fraction of matmul time

params.name: r
params.label: exp ops per clock per SM

scenes.caption: With 16 exp ops per clock per SM (H100 and B200), at $d = 128$ the exponentials cost 0.5 of the matmul time on H100 and 1.0 on B200. If they run in series with the matmuls, they cap utilization.
The FlashAttention-4 paper notes B300/GB300 double MUFU to 32 ops per clock per SM, which halves the curves. Smaller head dimensions are worse: less matmul work per exponential.

blocks.md: Misconception: "attention is two GEMMs, so it runs at GEMM speed." The softmax between them is cheap in FLOPs but runs on units hundreds of times slower than the tensor cores. FP8 makes it worse: matmul throughput doubles while exponential throughput stays the same.

blocks.title: Reported best forward throughput as % of dense peak

scenes.caption: Utilization = reported TFLOPs/s divided by the stated peak: 230/312 = 73.7% on A100, about 35% on H100 (as reported), 740/989 = 74.8% for FA3, 1613/2250 = 71.7% for FA4. Each new GPU resets the kernel back to low utilization until it is redesigned.

blocks.question: On H100 at $d = 128$, exponentials take about 50% of the matmul time. If FP8 matmuls run at 2x the FP16 rate and MUFU is unchanged, what does that ratio become?
options: 25%, because FP8 values are half the size
50%, unchanged
About 100%
About 200%
blocks.explain: $T_{exp}/T_{MMA} = r_{MMA}/(4 d\, r_{exp})$. Doubling $r_{MMA}$ doubles the ratio from 0.5 to 1.0: the exponentials now take as long as the matmuls. The FlashAttention-3 paper says exactly this: "the matmul throughput doubles but the exponential throughput stays the same."

blocks.question: Why is the fused kernel's ideal arithmetic intensity $N/2$ FLOPs per byte rather than a constant?
options: Because FLOPs grow as $N^2 d$ while unique bytes (Q, K, V, O) grow only as $N d$
Because longer sequences use larger tiles
Because the softmax is cheaper for long rows
Because HBM bandwidth increases with $N$
blocks.explain: $4N^2 d$ FLOPs over $8Nd$ bytes (4 matrices, 2 bytes each) is $N/2$. The naive kernel instead moves $\Theta(N^2)$ bytes for $\Theta(N^2 d)$ FLOPs, so its intensity is stuck near a constant (about $d/2$), which is why it stays memory bound at every length.

lessons.title: FlashAttention-3: producer and consumer warps, then ping-pong

blocks.md: FlashAttention-3 (Shah, Bikshandi, Zhang, Thakkar, Ramani and Dao, 2024) targets the Hopper H100. Three Hopper features matter. The **Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA)** is a hardware unit that copies tiles between HBM and shared memory (SMEM, the 228 KiB per-SM scratchpad) asynchronously. **WGMMA** is Hopper's tensor-core instruction: it is issued by a **warpgroup** (4 warps, 128 threads), reads operands straight from SMEM, and runs asynchronously, so the issuing threads can keep working. And **setmaxnreg** lets warpgroups give registers to each other at run time.

Asynchrony enables **warp specialization**: a thread block's warps are split into roles that only ever issue one kind of work. In FlashAttention-3, a **producer** warpgroup issues TMA loads of the $K_j$ and $V_j$ tiles into an $s$-stage circular buffer in SMEM, and **consumer** warpgroups issue WGMMAs and do the softmax. Barriers say when a stage is full (consumer may read) and when it is free again (producer may overwrite).

blocks.title: Producer and consumer sharing a 2-stage SMEM buffer

scenes.caption: The producer frees most of its registers (one thread is enough to issue TMA) and starts loads for $Q_i$ and the first tiles. It does not wait for any load to finish before issuing the next.

add.label: TMA: Q_i, K0, V0 to stage 0

scenes.caption: When a load lands, a barrier tells the consumer stage 0 is full. The consumer, which received the extra registers, runs $S = Q_i K_0^\top$ as an SS-GEMM (both operands from SMEM).
Done with $K_0, V_0$, the consumer releases stage 0. Only then may the producer reuse it, here for $K_2, V_2$. Meanwhile stage 1 is already loaded, so the consumer never waits on HBM.
At the end the consumer divides by $l$, computes $L = m + \log l$ and writes $O_i$ and $L_i$ to HBM. Loads and math overlapped the whole time, with no warp doing both.

add.label: O = O / l, L = m + log l

blocks.md: Why move registers? The producer only issues TMA, for which a single thread suffices, while consumers hold the $S$ and $O$ accumulators in registers. setmaxnreg shifts the register budget to the warps that do math, which allows larger tiles.

Warp specialization overlaps loads with math. It does not overlap the softmax with the matmuls of the same warpgroup. **Ping-pong scheduling** does that across two consumer warpgroups: named barriers (`bar.sync`) force warpgroup 1's GEMMs (PV of this iteration plus $QK^\top$ of the next) to issue before warpgroup 2's. So warpgroup 1 runs its softmax while warpgroup 2 occupies the tensor cores, then the roles swap. The idea is adapted from CUTLASS's ping-pong GEMM.

blocks.title: Simplified model: GEMM = 1 unit each, softmax = 1 unit

scenes.caption: One consumer, no overlap: QK, then softmax, then PV. Softmax costs half of the two GEMMs (the H100 ratio at $d = 128$), so the tensor cores sit idle 4 of every 12 units: 67% busy.

Ping-pong with two warpgroups: each warpgroup's softmax runs while the other's GEMMs hold the tensor cores. In this idealized model they stay 100% busy and finish 12 GEMM units in the time the serial schedule did 8.

blocks.md: The real gain is smaller than the idealized model because instruction issue, barriers and register limits get in the way. The paper reports that ping-pong took FP16 forward at head dimension 128 and sequence length 8192 from 570 to 620 to 640 TFLOPs/s, that is from 57.6% to about 63 to 65% of the 989 TFLOPS peak.

blocks.question: In ping-pong scheduling, what is warpgroup 2 doing while warpgroup 1 computes its softmax?
options: Waiting at a barrier until warpgroup 1 finishes
Running its GEMMs (PV of one iteration and QK of the next) on the tensor cores
Issuing TMA loads for the next K and V tiles
Computing its own softmax on the multi-function unit
blocks.explain: The barriers order the two warpgroups' GEMMs so that one warpgroup's slow softmax (exp on MUFU) lands under the other's tensor-core work. Loading is the producer warpgroup's job, and running both softmaxes at once would just make them compete for MUFU.

blocks.question: A teammate proposes giving the producer warpgroup as many registers as the consumers, "to be fair." What is the most likely effect?
options: Faster loads, because TMA needs registers for each byte copied
No effect, because register counts are fixed per kernel
Fewer registers for the consumers, forcing smaller tiles or spills in the math path
Better ping-pong, because both warpgroups can then do softmax
blocks.explain: TMA is issued by a single thread and copies data without staging it in registers. Registers given to the producer are taken from the consumers, which hold the accumulators; the paper deallocates producer registers and reallocates them to consumers for exactly this reason.

lessons.title: FlashAttention-3 inside a warpgroup, and FP8 done accurately

blocks.md: Within one warpgroup the loop body is a dependency chain: softmax needs $S_j = Q_i K_j^\top$, and $P_j V_j$ needs the softmax output. FlashAttention-3 breaks the chain by pipelining **across** iterations. Because WGMMA is asynchronous, the warpgroup can issue $Q_i K_{j}^\top$ for the next block and $\tilde P_{cur} V_{j-1}$ for the previous one, then run the softmax on the new scores while the $PV$ GEMM is still executing on the tensor cores.

blocks.code:
# Consumer warpgroup, 2-stage pipeline (simplified from Algorithm 2)
S_cur = wgmma(Q_i, K[0]); wait()
m, P_cur, l = softmax_step(S_cur)
for j in range(1, Tc):
    S_next = wgmma(Q_i, K[j])        # issue, do not wait
    O = O + wgmma(P_cur, V[j-1])     # issue, do not wait
    wait(S_next)
    m, P_next, l = softmax_step(S_next)  # overlaps the PV GEMM
    wait(O); O = rescale(O)
    release(K[j], V[j-1])
    P_cur = P_next
O = O + wgmma(P_cur, V[Tc-1]); wait()
O = O / l
blocks.caption: Paraphrase of the paper's Algorithm 2; real code also handles masking, FP32 to FP16 conversion and barriers.

blocks.title: One warpgroup, 4 iterations: serial vs 2-stage pipeline

scenes.caption: Serial: each iteration costs 3 units (QK, softmax, PV) and 4 iterations take 12. Simplified model with every step costing 1 unit.

2-stage: softmax of block $j$ runs while PV of block $j-1$ is on the tensor cores. Each steady-state iteration costs 2 units, so the same work ends at 9. Idealized: the compiler must not undo the ordering.

blocks.md: The overlap is not free. The pipeline keeps an extra $S_{next}$ in registers, $B_r \times B_c \times 4$ bytes per thread block: with $B_r = B_c = 128$ that is 64 KiB, a quarter of the SM's 256 KiB register file. That competes with large tiles, which are also register hungry. The authors also tried a 3-stage version; it needed even more registers and the compiler only overlapped one of the two GEMMs, so it performed worse than 2-stage.

blocks.title: Ablation: FP16, batch 4, seqlen 8448, 16 heads, d = 128

scenes.caption: Removing either technique costs 12 to 14%: 570 and 582 vs 661 TFLOPs/s, or 57.6%, 58.8% and 66.8% of the 989 TFLOPS peak. Check: $4 \cdot 8448^2 \cdot 128 \cdot 16 \cdot 4 / 3.538\text{ ms} = 661$. The headline 740 (75%) comes from other shapes.

blocks.md: **FP8.** Hopper's FP8 tensor cores have twice the FP16 throughput per SM. Two problems follow. First, layout: FP8 WGMMA requires operands contiguous in the inner (k) dimension, but V is usually stored contiguous in the head dimension, so FlashAttention-3 transposes each V tile inside the kernel with the LDSM and STSM instructions, and permutes the registers of the first GEMM's FP32 accumulator so it can feed the second GEMM. Second, accuracy: FP8 e4m3 has only 3 mantissa bits, and LLM activations have outliers.

Two techniques fix the accuracy. **Block quantization** keeps one scale per $B_r \times d$ or $B_c \times d$ block of Q, K and V instead of one per tensor, and since the kernel works on blocks anyway, applying the scales costs nothing. **Incoherent processing** multiplies Q and K by the same random orthogonal matrix $M$ before quantizing. Because $MM^\top = I$, the scores are unchanged, but each entry of $QM$ is a mix of many entries, so an outlier gets spread out. FlashAttention-3 uses a Hadamard matrix times a random $\pm 1$ diagonal, which costs $O(d \log d)$ and can be fused into the rotary embedding.

blocks.caption: Incoherent processing does not change attention scores, only how they are quantized.

blocks.title: A query with an outlier, before and after a 4x4 rotation

scenes.caption: Original vectors. $q$ has one outlier (8.0) and three small entries, so one entry sets the shared FP8 scale and the magnitudes are very uneven. Max/RMS of $q$ is 1.99. Toy numbers.
After $M = DH$ (a $\pm 1$ diagonal times the normalized 4x4 Hadamard): $qM = (4.3, -4, -3.5, 4.2)$, max/RMS 1.07, so every entry uses the FP8 range well. $kM = (0.7, 0.3, -0.4, 0.2)$.
The dot product is preserved: $q \cdot k = 4.05$ and $(qM)\cdot(kM) = 4.05$. Attention scores are unchanged before quantization; only the rounding error changes.

blocks.title: FP8 attention RMSE vs FP64 reference (x 0.001, outlier test)

scenes.caption: Inputs are $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ plus a rare $\mathcal{N}(0,100)$ outlier term on 0.1% of entries. FA3 FP8 reaches 9.1e-3 vs 24e-3 for the baseline: $24/9.1 = 2.6$x lower error.
The ablations show which part matters on this test: dropping block quantization barely changes the error (9.3e-3), while dropping incoherent processing returns it to the baseline (24e-3).

blocks.md: FP8 FlashAttention-3 was released for the forward pass only (FP16 and BF16 have forward and backward), and the paper's FP8 kernel lacked the persistent-kernel load balancing of the FP16 one, so it trailed cuDNN's FP8 kernels for short sequences and causal masking. It reached close to 1.2 PFLOPs/s, about 60% of an FP8 peak taken as twice the FP16 peak.

blocks.question: Why does multiplying both Q and K by a random orthogonal matrix reduce FP8 error without changing the attention output?
options: It shrinks every value toward zero, so rounding errors are smaller
Scores are preserved because $MM^\top = I$, and mixing entries spreads outliers so one scale fits all entries better
It sorts the head dimension so outliers end up in a single block that is kept in FP16
It converts the values to integers, which FP8 represents exactly
blocks.explain: Orthogonality keeps $QK^\top$ identical. Each rotated entry is a signed sum of many original entries, which evens out magnitudes (max/RMS fell from 1.99 to 1.07 in the toy example), so quantization with a shared scale loses less information.

blocks.question: Your FA3-style kernel spills registers after you enlarge the key block size $B_c$ from 128 to 176. Which part of the 2-stage pipeline is most directly to blame?
options: The extra $S_{next}$ buffer of $B_r \times B_c$ FP32 values kept in registers
The TMA descriptors, which grow with $B_c$
The circular SMEM buffer, which lives in registers
The log-sum-exp vector, which grows with $B_c$
blocks.explain: The paper calls out exactly this tradeoff: the 2-stage pipeline holds an extra $S_{next}$ of size $B_r \times B_c \times$ sizeof(float) per thread block, which competes with larger block sizes. SMEM buffers are not in registers, and the log-sum-exp has one value per query row ($B_r$), not per key.

lessons.title: FlashAttention-4 forward: when the exponential is the bottleneck

blocks.md: FlashAttention-4 (Zadouri, Hoehnerbach, Shah, Liu, Thakkar and Dao, 2026) targets Blackwell B200 and GB200. Its premise is **asymmetric scaling**: B200 BF16 tensor cores do 8192 ops per clock per SM, twice Hopper's 4096 (2.25 vs about 1 PFLOPS per GPU), while MUFU stays at 16 exponentials per clock per SM and shared memory reads stay at 128 bytes per clock per SM. FlashAttention-3 does not run on B200 at all: Hopper's WGMMA instructions are not forward compatible.

Blackwell also brings new hardware. **Tensor memory (TMEM)** is 256 KB per SM of on-chip storage wired to the tensor cores, so MMA results land there instead of in registers. The 5th-generation MMA (`tcgen05.mma`) is fully asynchronous, launched by a single thread, works on $128 \times N$ tiles (vs $64 \times N$ on Hopper), and can read operand A from TMEM. A **2-CTA** mode lets two thread blocks (CTAs) in a cluster execute one MMA together.
The paper starts with a per-tile roofline ("feeds and speeds"). For a query tile of $M$ rows, a key tile of $N$ columns and head dimension $d$, all multiples of 128:

blocks.caption: Shared-memory time counts operands re-read by multiple 128-wide MMA instructions, at 2 bytes per element and 128 bytes per cycle.

blocks.title: B200 forward roofline per tile (clock cycles)

scenes.caption: $M = N = d = 128$: MMA $4 \cdot 128^3/8192 = 1024$, SMEM 768, exp $128^2/16 = 1024$. The exponentials take as long as both matmuls together, so any serialization halves throughput.
$M = 256$ (two 128-row query tiles): 2048, 1536 and 2048. Larger tiles do not change the balance; exp still ties the tensor cores.
Illustrative, not from the paper: if 20% of the exponentials move to the FMA units (FA4 emulates 10 to 25%), MUFU work for the 128 tile drops from 1024 to 819 cycles, under the MMA time.

blocks.md: **The pipeline.** Each CTA computes two 128-row query tiles, $Q^H$ and $Q^L$, in ping-pong as in FlashAttention-3. Because the $128 \times 128$ score tile sits in TMEM and is read out one row per thread, each 128-thread softmax warpgroup owns one tile, with one full row per thread, so no shuffles are needed for the row max. The two softmax warpgroups are synchronized so their exponential phases do not overlap. $P$ goes back to TMEM in stages (three quarters, then the last quarter) to limit register pressure, and the PV MMA starts as soon as the first chunk is stored.

blocks.title: FlashAttention-4 forward: warp roles in one CTA

scenes.caption: TMA brings K and V tiles into SMEM; a single thread launches MMAs whose results go to TMEM, not registers. That freed register file is what makes 128-element rows per thread affordable.
The two softmax warpgroups read rows of S from TMEM, compute exponentials, and write P back for the PV MMA. They take turns on the exponential phase so they do not fight over MUFU.
A dedicated correction warpgroup rescales $O$ in TMEM when the running max changes, which takes rescaling off the softmax critical path. At the end it normalizes and writes $O$ and $L$.

blocks.md: **Software exponential.** Kernels compute $e^x$ as $2^{x \log_2 e}$, and FlashAttention-4 evaluates some of those $2^x$ on the FMA units, which would otherwise idle, in parallel with MUFU. It uses Cody-Waite range reduction, $2^x = 2^{\lfloor x \rfloor} \cdot 2^{x - \lfloor x \rfloor}$: the integer part becomes exponent bits, and the fractional part is a degree-3 polynomial evaluated with Horner's method. The coefficients come from the Sollya tool.

blocks.title: Emulated 2^x for the score s - m = -2
blocks.code:
def exp2_emulated(x):
    x = max(x, -127.0)        # avoid underflow
    n = floor(x)              # GPU: add 2^23 + 2^22, round down
    f = x - n                 # fractional part in [0, 1)
    p = ((0.0771*f + 0.2276)*f + 0.6951)*f + 1.0
    return ldexp(p, n)        # shift n into the exponent bits

scenes.caption: The score $-2$ from lesson 1 (block 1's 1 minus max 3) becomes $x = -2 \log_2 e = -2.8854$, so we want $2^x = e^{-2} = 0.135335$.
Range reduction: $n = -3$ and $f = 0.1146$, so only $2^f$ on $[0, 1)$ needs a polynomial.
Three fused multiply-adds evaluate the polynomial. Coefficients rounded to 4 digits here; the code uses full FP32 values.
Putting $n$ into the exponent gives 0.135346, a relative error of $8.2 \times 10^{-5}$, far below BF16's own rounding step of about $3.9 \times 10^{-3}$.

blocks.md: The paper measures the degree-3 polynomial at a maximum relative error of $8.8 \times 10^{-5}$ in FP32, about 600x worse than MUFU, but after rounding to BF16 the two are indistinguishable (within 1 BF16 ulp, one step between adjacent BF16 values, on 99% of inputs). Emulation costs registers and latency, so only 10 to 25% of each row is emulated; the rest still uses `MUFU.EX2`. The repo's tuning table sets this split per configuration.

**Conditional rescaling.** Rescaling $O$ is only needed when the max grows, and a little slack is harmless as long as the final division uses consistent statistics. FlashAttention-4 rescales only when the max jumps by more than a threshold $\tau$; otherwise it keeps the old max. The code sets $\tau = 8$ in log2 units (a factor of $2^8 = 256$) for 16-bit inputs and 0 for FP8, and the decision is made per warp to avoid divergence.

blocks.tex: O_j = \begin{cases} e^{m_{j-1}-m_j}\, O_{j-1} + e^{S_j - m_j} V_j & \text{if } m_j - m_{j-1} > \tau \\ O_{j-1} + e^{S_j - m_{j-1}} V_j & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
blocks.caption: From the FlashAttention-4 paper (the code compares the jump in log2 units).

blocks.prompt: Rerun the lesson 1 example with this rule. Block 2 raises the max from 3 to 5, a jump of $2 \log_2 e = 2.885$ in log2 units. Does FlashAttention-4 rescale, and is the final answer still 42.347?
blocks.reveal: **No rescale, same answer.** $2.885 < 8$, so the kernel keeps $m = 3$. Block 2's weights become $e^{2-3} = 0.3679$ and $e^{5-3} = 7.389$ (bigger than 1, which is fine), block 3's are 0.0821 and 2.7183. Then $l = 11.6926$ and $O = 495.15$, and $O/l = 42.347$, exactly as before. Zero rescale operations instead of one.

scenes.caption: Block 1 is identical to plain online softmax: $m = 3$, $l = 1.1353$, $O = 21.353$.
Block 2's max is 5, a jump of 2.885 log2 units, below 8. No rescale: weights are taken against $m = 3$, so the 5 gives $e^{2} = 7.389$. $l = 8.8923$, $O = 327.95$.
Block 3 adds 0.0821 and 2.7183: $l = 11.693$, $O = 495.15$. Dividing gives 42.347, the exact answer. Values up to $2^8$ larger than usual are why $\tau$ must keep $P$ inside the input type's range.

blocks.md: The threshold is not free slack. Skipping a rescale lets unnormalized weights grow up to $2^\tau$, and $P$ is cast to the input type before $PV$. The code asserts that the offset plus $\tau$ stays below $\log_2$ of the type's largest value, and uses $\tau = 0$ for FP8, whose maximum is only 448.

blocks.question: Why does FlashAttention-4 emulate only 10 to 25% of exponentials in software instead of all of them?
options: The polynomial is too inaccurate for more than a quarter of the row
Emulation uses extra registers, register bandwidth and latency; doing all of them would cause spills and leave MUFU idle
FMA units can only process one row in four
MUFU is faster than the FMA units for every input
blocks.explain: The goal is to split the work between two units that can run in parallel. The paper says full emulation would raise register pressure and could cause spills that cancel the gain, so the fraction is tuned to the MMA-to-exp ratio of each tile shape. Accuracy is not the limit: after BF16 rounding the polynomial matches hardware.

blocks.question: According to the per-tile roofline, which resources bound the B200 forward pass at $M = N = d = 128$?
options: Shared memory bandwidth alone
HBM bandwidth
Tensor cores and the exponential unit, tied at 1024 cycles each
Integer ALUs used for masking
blocks.explain: MMA and exp are both 1024 cycles; shared memory is 768. This is why the forward pass's design centers on overlapping softmax with MMA and on reducing exp and rescaling work. Shared memory becomes the bottleneck in the backward pass.

lessons.title: FlashAttention-4 backward, scheduling, and using the kernels

blocks.md: The backward pass runs five MMAs per tile: recompute $S = QK^\top$, then $dP = dO\,V^\top$, $dV = P^\top dO$, $dK = dS^\top Q$ and $dQ = dS\,K$. Each thread block owns a K/V tile and loops over query tiles, so $dK$ and $dV$ accumulate locally, but $dQ$ for a query tile receives contributions from every K/V tile and is summed with atomic adds in HBM.

With $M = N = d = 128$ the paper's roofline gives 2560 cycles of MMA, 1024 of exponential, and 3328 of shared memory traffic: 2048 for MMA operands, 256 to write $dS$, and 1024 to write $dQ$ in FP32 and read it back for the reduction. Shared memory, not math, is the limit, by 30%.

scenes.caption: 1-CTA, $M = N = d = 128$: SMEM total 3328 vs 2560 for the tensor cores ($3328/2560 = 1.3$).
2-CTA mode ($M = 256$ split over a CTA pair): operand traffic falls to 1536 and dQ traffic to 512, at the cost of 384 cycles of distributed shared memory exchange. Total 2688, only 5% above MMA.

blocks.md: Two ideas get there. First, **TMEM**: FlashAttention-3 held accumulators in registers, which forced an almost serial order (S, dP, dV, dQ, dK). FlashAttention-4 keeps intermediates in TMEM, recomputes the tiles transposed ($S^\top$, $P^\top$) so they sit in TMEM in exactly the operand layout the dV and dK MMAs read, and overlaps the dK and dQ MMAs of the previous tile with the softmax work of the current one. TMEM cannot hold five accumulators, so S and P share one region and dP, dS and dQ share another.

Second, **2-CTA MMA**: with tile $M = 256$, each CTA of the pair stages only half of operand B in its own SMEM. The dQ MMA reduces over the key dimension, which the pair has split, so the CTAs swap halves of $dS$ through distributed shared memory (DSMEM). Each CTA then owns $M/2$ rows with the full $2N$ reduction and writes only half of the dQ tile, which also halves the number of global atomic adds.

scenes.caption: Each CTA stages only half of operand B; the paired MMA reads both halves. That is where the operand traffic drop from 2048 to 1536 cycles comes from.
For dQ the reduction axis is split across the pair, so the CTAs exchange halves of $dS$ over DSMEM. That costs 384 cycles in the roofline, much less than it saves.
Each CTA now writes only its half of the dQ tile, so the pair issues half as many global atomic adds as two independent CTAs would.

blocks.md: Atomic adds make dQ (and dK, dV with grouped-query attention) nondeterministic: floating point addition order changes run to run. FlashAttention-4 offers a **deterministic mode** that serializes the reductions with a semaphore in a fixed order, using CTA swizzling and a shortest-processing-time-first order for causal masks to limit stalls. The paper reports up to 75% of the nondeterministic 1-CTA speed; the later blog post reports 85 to 90%.

**Scheduling.** With causal masking, query tiles near the start of the sequence have short loops and tiles near the end have long ones. Launched in the natural order, SMs pick up the short tiles first and the long ones last, leaving a ragged tail. FlashAttention-4 uses **longest-processing-time-first (LPT)** ordering, swizzling heads into sections that fit in L2 cache. It works on any GPU: the authors measured 4 to 8% gains for MHA and 7 to 14% for MQA on an H200 with FlashAttention-3. For variable-length batches, a preprocessing kernel sorts batches by cost.

blocks.title: Toy causal workload: 4 tiles of length 1 to 4 on 2 SMs

scenes.caption: Natural order (shortest first), each tile going to the first free SM: the longest tile starts last and the job ends at 6 units, with SM 1 idle for the last 2.
Longest first: SM 1 takes 4 then 1, SM 2 takes 3 then 2, and both finish at 5. Same work, about 17% less wall time, with no change to the kernel's math.

blocks.md: **Implementation and results.** FlashAttention-4 is written entirely in CuTe-DSL, the Python-embedded DSL of CUTLASS, which compiles to PTX and then to machine code. Compiling one kernel took 2.5 s for the forward and 1.4 s for the backward, versus 55 s and 45 s for FlashAttention-3's C++ templates (22x and 32x faster). On B200 with BF16 the paper reports up to 1613 TFLOPs/s, 71.7% of 2.25 PFLOPS, 1.1 to 1.3x faster than cuDNN 9.13 and 2.1 to 2.7x faster than Triton in the forward pass. The authors note that newer cuDNN releases have since adopted many of these techniques and perform similarly.

# FlashAttention-3 (Hopper): built from the repo's hopper/ directory
from flash_attn_3 import flash_attn_interface
out = flash_attn_interface.flash_attn_func(q, k, v, causal=True)

# FlashAttention-4 (CuTe-DSL, Hopper and Blackwell): pip install flash-attn-4
from flash_attn.cute import flash_attn_func
out, lse = flash_attn_func(q, k, v, causal=True)  # returns (out, lse)
blocks.caption: Entry points as documented in the Dao-AILab/flash-attention README. q, k, v are (batch, seqlen, heads, head_dim) tensors on the GPU. Check the README for current requirements.

blocks.md: Each generation chases the bottleneck the previous hardware exposed. FlashAttention removed HBM traffic for $S$ and $P$. FlashAttention-2 fixed work partitioning. FlashAttention-3 used Hopper's asynchrony to hide softmax and loads under the matmuls. FlashAttention-4 attacks the exponential unit and shared memory bandwidth, which stopped scaling with Blackwell's tensor cores.

blocks.question: What is the main reason FlashAttention-4 uses the 2-CTA MMA mode in the backward pass?
options: To double the tensor core FLOPs available to each CTA
To cut shared memory traffic (each CTA stages half of operand B) and halve dQ atomic adds
To make the backward pass deterministic
To fit five accumulators in tensor memory
blocks.explain: The backward pass is limited by shared memory bandwidth (3328 vs 2560 cycles). Pairing CTAs means each stages half of B, and the dS exchange lets each CTA own half of the dQ tile, halving atomics. Peak FLOPs are unchanged, and determinism comes from the separate semaphore mode.

blocks.question: A varlen inference batch contains short prefills followed by a few very long-context decodes. Which FlashAttention-4 scheduling idea addresses the resulting slowdown?
options: Conditional softmax rescaling
Sorting batches by their per-tile cost so the longest work starts first (LPT)
Emulating the exponential on FMA units
Switching to FP8
blocks.explain: This is load imbalance: if long work is processed last, a few SMs finish late while others sit idle. The paper launches a small preprocessing kernel to sort batches by cost and write a virtual-to-actual batch index map, which can be cached so sorting costs nothing on later calls.
